newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU defuses EMU row with promises on paper.
newsitem.headline: EU defuses EMU row with promises on paper.

text.p: The European Union found the right words on Monday to plug a gaping division in the way it views economic and monetary union (EMU), staving off a potential crisis in its plans for a single currency.

With deceptive ease, finance ministers presented their leaders at the EU's mid-year summit with a resolution on economic growth and employment that met France's concerns that the bloc was too intent on fiscal austerity.
The resolution along with another on economic stability, will go along with the bloc's stability pact, a framework for ensuring that budgets stay under control after EMU is launched in January 1999.
Resolutions from EU leaders carry no legal weight but give strong political signals to officials.
The employment resolution called for stronger links between EMU and jobs, for enhanced cooperation between EU states in employment policy, and for tax policy to be used to stimulate employment.
In one of its more concrete actions, it called on the European Investment Bank, the bloc's main lending institution, to open up its loans to small businesses that specialise in high-technology.

A special European Union summit on jobs was also likely later this year in the autumn to keep the issue of unemployment high on the EU's agenda. Luxembourg, which will host the summit, insisted that it serve some real purpose.
Officials hailed the agreement as a sign that all was well with monetary union.
"There are only winners. No losers," Dutch Finance Minister Gerrit Zalm said after the resolution was agreed.
But the row itself left Europe's division about how the euro would be managed after EMU is launched on January 1, 1999, relatively unresolved.

The latest crisis in the EU's plans for a single currency erupted last week when France's new Socialist government held up routine agreement of the stability pact, which it said did not do anything for the bloc's jobless lines.
Paris wants more political control over economic issues and is keen to see jobs creation given a higher role. Germany is vehemently committed to budgetary discipline and wary of government intrusion.
Bonn fought hard to stop any money being allocated for job creation programmes.

Financial analysts shrugged off the deal. Brian Venables, a senior bond analyst at ABN AMBRO, said the agreement underlined that EMU would go ahead, probably with a broad group of countries. "What can derail it now?" he said.
Robert Hayward of Bank of America said France and Germany had to agree or see EMU fail. But he said it was a fudge.
"It lets France go back and say we have done something and the Germans go back and say we haven't given in to anything, he said.
